name: Question 16
problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-6y=6{e}^{3x}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-3x},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{3x}$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{3x}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{3x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{3x})^{′}=3{e}^{3x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(3{e}^{3x})^{′}=9{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(9{e}^{3x})+(3{e}^{3x})-6({e}^{3x})=6{e}^{3x}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{3x}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{3x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x{e}^{3x})^{′}={e}^{3x}+3x{e}^{3x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{3x}+3x{e}^{3x})^{′}=6{e}^{3x}+9x{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(6{e}^{3x}+9x{e}^{3x})+({e}^{3x}+3x{e}^{3x})-6(x{e}^{3x})=6{e}^{3x}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{3x}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-3x}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-3x}+{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=e3x, we have y′(x)=(e3x)′=3e3x,y″(x)=(3e3x)′=9e3x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (9e3x)+(3e3x)−6(e3x)=6e3x.✓ So, yp(x)=e3x is a particular solution of the differential equation.

  • For yp(x)=xe3x, we have y′(x)=(xe3x)′=e3x+3xe3x,y″(x)=(e3x+3xe3x)′=6e3x+9xe3x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (6e3x+9xe3x)+(e3x+3xe3x)−6(xe3x)=6e3x.× So, yp(x)=xe3x isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Ae2x+Be−3x. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Ae2x+Be−3x+e3x where A and B are arbitrary constants.
